replies.text:
Checks (step 2):
- Automated abuse of reachable endpoints: design says "Pull requests can come from forks by anyone on the internet" and every PR triggers a review — covered by listed threat 4 (unbounded LLM cost).
- Privileged screens showing other people's content: the bot "posts comments" read by maintainers; attacker diff text could be laundered into a trusted bot comment — effectively covered by listed threat 3 (bot output misleading humans).
- Approving/merging with no record of who did it: design says "it can approve pull requests when it finds no issues" and "The bot's token can approve and merge" — not covered; the confirmed list contains no Repudiation threat.
- Personal/financial documents cacheable by browsers/CDNs: design has no such pages — not applicable.
- Attacker text ending up in logs, exports, emails or another interpreting system: design mentions only PR comments, no logs/exports/email — not applicable.
- Single-reviewer item 1 (code egress to the external model provider): real and quoted — "A bot reviews every pull request with an LLM" with deterministic signal exposure internal; distinct from listed threat 1 (which is about echoing files back into a public fork PR). Include.
- Single-reviewer item 3 (approval satisfies human review gate) is a consequence of listed threats 3/5 — excluded.

{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-02",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["review bot", "LLM provider", "pull request host", "bot token"],
    "dataStores": ["repository files"],
    "externalServices": ["LLM provider"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["fork contributor to bot", "bot to external LLM"],
    "dataClasses": ["secrets"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": true
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "All private repository code is sent to an external LLM provider on every pull request",
      "scenario": "The bot sends the full diff plus the repository's files to an external LLM for every pull request, with no stated gate on which repositories or file types are included. Any employee opening a routine pull request, or any outsider opening a fork pull request, causes proprietary source, config and any credentials living in those files to leave the organisation to a third-party model provider, where it may be retained or used for training. No attacker interaction with the bot's prompt is needed.",
      "component": "review bot to external LLM provider",
      "likelihood": 5,
      "impact": 4,
      "rating": { "attacker": "insider", "effort": "low", "reach": "all", "harm": "sensitive_data" },
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "A bot reviews every pull request with an LLM and posts comments. It reads the diff and the repository’s files" },
        { "quote": "\"exposure\":\"internal\",\"llmFeatures\":true" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V1.8.2"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "Every pull request ships your private code and config files to an outside AI service, with no rule about what may be sent.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Gate and minimise what the review bot sends to the external model",
        "given": "a pull request in a private or internal repository",
        "when": "the bot assembles context for the LLM",
        "then": "only explicitly allow-listed repositories and file paths are sent, secrets and excluded paths are stripped, the provider is contractually bound to no-retention/no-training, and the egress is recorded"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "Bot approvals and merges leave no record of what decided them",
      "scenario": "The bot approves and merges using a single shared token, so a merge of attacker-controlled code appears only as the bot. The design records no link between a verdict and the pull request content, prompt and model output that produced it. After an incident nobody can tell whether the bot was hijacked by injected diff text, which other pull requests got the same treatment, or whether a person with access to the token merged code under the bot's identity, so abuse goes unseen and is deniable.",
      "component": "review bot approve/merge action",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "rating": { "attacker": "insider", "effort": "low", "reach": "all", "harm": "minor" },
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "it can approve pull requests when it finds no issues" },
        { "quote": "The bot’s token can approve and merge." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V7.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-778"],
      "plainLanguage": "When the bot approves or merges code, nothing records why or on whose behalf, so a hijacked or misused bot cannot be traced afterwards.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Audit every automated approval and merge",
        "given": "the bot approves or merges a pull request",
        "when": "the action is taken with the bot token",
        "then": "an append-only audit record is written linking the action to the pull request revision, the prompt and model output hash, the model version and the triggering event, and the records are retained and reviewable"
      }
    }
  ]
}
